title: MIT Just Called Time of Death on the Take-Home Assignment
author: How to Teach With AI
source: How to Teach With AI (howtoteachwithai.substack.com), August 28, 2026
summary: Responding to MIT's committee report concluding that AI can now do MIT-level work, making the traditional out-of-class assessment machine (problem sets, take-home exams, essays) unable to measure real learning, the author lays out a five-principle 'mastery learning' system already running in their own classroom as a practical answer. The five principles are: time is the variable while mastery stays the constant (students revise until work meets a fixed bar rather than being graded once on a schedule); feedback, not grades, is the currency of the course; outside practitioners rather than the instructor render the verdict on whether work is real; class time is reserved for productive struggle rather than content delivery, since AI can explain content anytime; and every artifact must be accompanied by a process log documenting the student's thinking, drafts, and AI use. The piece argues AI use is not banned but structured as a 'sparring partner, never a vending machine,' with oral defense of the process log serving as the check against AI having done the actual thinking. Each principle comes with a 'smallest version' the author recommends any teacher can start within 24 hours on a single assignment.
points: The 'cognitive surrender' framing from MIT's report — students producing stronger polished work while building less underlying capability — reframes rising output quality as a warning sign rather than a success metric when AI is involved.

Shifting the locus of assessment from the professor to outside practitioners ('an investigative reporter or an emergency room nurse judges the customer interviews') removes the 'just tell me what you want' negotiation dynamic between student and grader that AI-polished work exploits.

The process log requirement — documenting what was tried, what feedback was received, and where AI helped or failed — is positioned as the artifact that actually proves learning, since 'the artifact alone proves nothing anymore' once AI can produce a polished final product.

Making time the variable and mastery the fixed bar (rather than the reverse, standard in the 'factory model') directly targets AI's specific strength — producing free, polished first drafts — by requiring iteration against a fixed standard rather than one-shot grading.
quotes: The report came out this month, and the conclusion is blunt: problem sets, take-home exams, essays, the whole out-of-class assessment machine no longer measures learning, because AI can do MIT-level work.

Their students are turning in stronger work and building less capability every semester. The report even has a name for what happens when a student hands the hard part to a machine: "cognitive surrender.
AI is exactly why this matters now. A polished first draft is free. A grade locked in on the first attempt teaches students to optimize the first attempt, and AI is very good at first attempts.

Every artifact in my courses gets assessed by someone who does the work for a living. An investigative reporter or an emergency room nurse judges the customer interviews. I coach, they assess. That line is hard.
My rule is that AI works as a sparring partner, never a vending machine. They argue with it, make it attack their assumptions, and use it to test whether their thinking survives contact.
The artifact shows the work. The log shows the thinking. And in the AI era, the thinking is the only thing worth grading, because the artifact alone proves nothing anymore.
